chapter_title: Considerations for Hollow Bar Soil Nails

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Hollow bar soil nails (HBSNs), introduced about 20 years ago, are advanced to full length with a sacrificial bit using grout as the drilling fluid, so drilling, grouting and tendon installation are one process. They suit collapsible soils, where grout injected while drilling keeps the hole open. Two Central Federal Lands Highway Division publications guide their use: Cadden et al. (2010), pullout tests, and Samtani and Nowatzki (2010), corrosion. The chapter supplements the earlier chapters.
sections.body: 10.1 Introduction (p. 265). HBSNs have grown in popularity since the technology was introduced about 20 years ago (Cadden et al. 2010). They are advanced through their full design length with a sacrificial bit using grout as the drilling fluid; drilling, grouting and tendon installation are one single process. Two Central Federal Lands Highway Division publications give guidance: 'Hollow Bar Soil Nails Pullout Test Program', Cadden et al. (2010); and 'Hollow Bar Soil Nails - Review of Corrosion Factors and Mitigation Practice', Samtani and Nowatzki (2010). HBSNs are particularly advantageous in collapsible soils, where simultaneous grout injection through the tendon keeps the hole from collapsing. Their installation, design and corrosion protection need special considerations, covered here as a supplement to the preceding chapters.
key_points: Drilling, grouting and tendon installation in one process; grout is the drilling fluid
Particularly advantageous in collapsible soils: grout injected while drilling keeps the hole open
Guidance: Cadden et al. (2010) pullout test program; Samtani and Nowatzki (2010) corrosion review
Supplements the preceding chapters with HBSN-specific considerations
sections.applicability: Hollow bar soil nails: what they are and where they suit.

sections.title: Installation
sections.summary: An oversized sacrificial bit with grout exit ports is advanced on the hollow tendon while grout is pumped continuously, supporting the hole and cooling the bit; grout return at the face must be kept for adequate bond. Water must not be used as drilling fluid (erratic, poor bond). Grout specific gravity 1.8 to 1.9; at least 1,500 psi at 3 days and 3,000 to 4,000 psi at 28 days (AASHTO T106/ASTM C109), sampled from the return. Long nails may use 1.4 to 1.6 drilling grout, then final grout until it returns to the face.
sections.body: 10.2 Installation (pp. 265-266). Each HBSN has an oversized, sacrificial drill bit with grout exit ports; grout pumped from the surface through the hollow core exits the bit as the tendon, acting as the rotary drill string, advances. Continuous pumping gives temporary support against hole instability and prevents bit overheating; the grout return must be maintained at the face during drilling, as it contributes to adequate soil-grout bond. Grout inside the tendon is under significant pressure and exits the bit at relatively high velocity and low pressure, undercutting the soil around the bit and carrying cuttings to the surface. Water should not be used as drilling fluid in a first stage, nor after switching to grout in a second stage once drill depth is reached; water has caused erratic and poor bond strengths. HBSN grout must have a specific gravity of 1.8 to 1.9; minimum compressive strength 1,500 psi at 3 days and 3,000 to 4,000 psi at 28 days, meeting AASHTO T106/ASTM C109; the test sample is taken from the grout returning from the hole. For longer nails, a lighter drilling grout (specific gravity 1.4 to 1.6) is often used for economy to advance the bar and carry spoils; once at depth, a heavier final grout is pumped through the bar and the nail is complete when it returns to the face, showing the drilling grout and spoils have been flushed.
key_points: Oversized sacrificial bit with grout exit ports; the tendon is the rotary drill string
Continuous grout pumping supports the hole and cools the bit; keep grout return at the face
No water as drilling fluid at any stage: erratic and poor bond strengths
Grout specific gravity 1.8-1.9; >= 1,500 psi at 3 days, 3,000-4,000 psi at 28 days (AASHTO T106/ASTM C109)
Grout test sample taken from the return flow
Long nails: drilling grout 1.4-1.6, then final grout until it returns to the face

sections.title: Bond Strength
sections.summary: In an FHWA-ADSC study, 37 HBSNs at four U.S. sites were tested beside gravity-grouted solid bar nails (Cadden et al. 2010; Table 10.1, bond from the nominal bit diameter, some tests short of failure). In granular soils HBSNs developed larger bond (larger grout body from undercutting and permeation, rougher interface), so gravity-grouted values are likely very conservative; micropile presumptive values (Sabatini et al. 2005) may suit SP and GP soils. In SM soils HBSN bond was similar to gravity-grouted nails. Bond is more sensitive to craftsmanship.
sections.body: 10.3 Bond Strength (pp. 266-267). Thirty-seven HBSNs were installed at four U.S. sites and tested in an investigation co-sponsored by FHWA and the International Association of Foundation Drilling (ADSC) (Cadden et al. 2010), to establish de-bonding procedures for proof-testing HBSNs and to build a bond strength database; gravity-grouted solid bar nails were tested at each site for comparison. Table 10.1 values use the nominal drill bit diameter, not the actual grout body diameter; some tests did not reach failure, so the HBSN ranges may be somewhat conservative; presumptive pressure-grouted micropile values (Sabatini et al. 2005) are given for comparison. HBSNs developed larger bond in granular soils than gravity-grouted solid bars, owing to the larger hole and grout body created by undercutting and grout permeation and to rougher grout-soil interface features; the gravity-grouted values in Table 10.1 are therefore likely very conservative for HBSNs in most cases. HBSN bond is more sensitive to craftsmanship and each Contractor's installation details than solid bar bond. Micropile presumptive values may be appropriate for HBSNs in SP and GP soils. In granular soils with significant fines (SM), average HBSN bond was similar to gravity-grouted nails, suggesting undercutting and permeation are less significant; in these and predominantly fine-grained soils, the presumptive values in Table 10.1 may be appropriate for preliminary design.
key_points: 37 HBSNs at four U.S. sites, FHWA-ADSC study (Cadden et al. 2010), with solid bar comparisons
Table 10.1 bond computed from the nominal drill bit diameter; some tests did not reach failure
Granular soils: HBSN bond larger (bigger grout body, rougher interface); gravity-grouted values very conservative
Micropile presumptive values (Sabatini et al. 2005) may suit HBSNs in SP and GP soils
SM soils: HBSN bond similar to gravity-grouted nails; Table 10.1 values for preliminary design
HBSN bond more sensitive to craftsmanship and installation details

sections.title: Corrosion Protection of HBSNs
sections.summary: Under the same ground, HBSNs carry higher corrosion risk than solid bars: installation damages epoxy and zinc coatings (soil contact, outgoing cuttings, centralizer impact), so no Chapter 7 coating can be shown to protect them reliably. The only protection is a bare bar with sacrificial steel, from the Fishman and Withiam (2011) metal loss model: X(um) = 80 (um/yr) x tf^0.8 (Eq 7.1); dloss = dbar - 2X (Eq 7.2). HBSNs are not recommended in aggressive soil (Table 7.2); design life typically 50 to 75 years.
sections.body: 10.4 Corrosion Protection of HBSNs (pp. 267-269). Subsections 10.4.1 Introduction to 10.4.3 Design Steps for Corrosion Protection of HBSNs.
key_points: Bare bar with sacrificial steel is the only HBSN protection; not recommended in aggressive soil
sections.applicability: Corrosion protection (sacrificial steel) design of hollow bar soil nails.

subsections.title: Introduction
subsections.summary: HBSN corrosion protection is controversial because the tendon is abraded during installation. Under the same ground, HBSNs carry higher corrosion risk than solid bars (Samtani and Nowatzki 2010): soil contact, outgoing cuttings and centralizer impact damage epoxy and zinc coatings, severely shortening their life. No Chapter 7 coating can be routinely shown to protect them, so a bare bar with sacrificial steel is the only method available; Fishman and Withiam (2011) metal loss models can estimate the loss.
subsections.body: 10.4.1 Introduction (pp. 267-268). One of the most controversial topics for HBSNs is the effectiveness of corrosion protection, because of the abrasion and friction on the tendon during installation. Samtani and Nowatzki (2010) evaluated parameters related to HBSN corrosion, summarized the protection practice of the time and gave guidance. Under the same subsurface conditions, HBSNs have higher corrosion risks than solid bars because their installation methods tend to deteriorate the protection: epoxy and zinc coatings are damaged by contact with the soil mass, erosion from the outgoing soil cuttings and impact with centralizers, so the effective service life of coatings may be severely shortened. Fishman and Withiam (2011) evaluated computational models for metal loss in soil reinforcement of retaining structures (mainly MSE walls), developed a methodology from improved models to predict performance over the service life, suggested changes to the AASHTO LRFD specifications, and introduced modified LRFD resistance factors for corrosion exposure; although focused on MSE walls, their models can estimate the time-rate of metal loss and future performance of HBSNs. Because of the damage to bar coatings during installation, it cannot be routinely demonstrated that any coating of Chapter 7 reliably protects the tendons; the only corrosion protection method currently available for HBSNs is a bare bar with sacrificial steel.
key_points: Same ground: HBSNs have higher corrosion risk than solid bars (Samtani and Nowatzki 2010)
Installation damages epoxy and zinc coatings: soil contact, outgoing cuttings, centralizer impact
Fishman and Withiam (2011) metal loss models can estimate HBSN metal loss
Only protection currently available: bare bar with sacrificial steel
subsections.applicability: Corrosion protection (sacrificial steel) design of hollow bar soil nails.

subsections.title: Sacrificial Steel
subsections.summary: Without soil nail specific studies, sacrificial steel for HBSNs follows the Fishman and Withiam (2011) metal loss model, built from uncoated mild steel wire and strips buried in MSE reinforced zones, where fill aggressiveness is controlled, with reduced tension resistance factors for material variability and model accuracy. Eq. 7.1: X(um) = 80 (um/yr) x tf^0.8; the loss is taken twice from the diameter, dloss = dbar - 2X (Eq. 7.2). The reduced diameter gives the steel area for Chapter 6 design, with the Chapter 5 and 6 tension resistance factors.
subsections.body: 10.4.2 Sacrificial Steel (pp. 268-269). In the absence of thorough studies specific to soil nail corrosion, the manual uses the metal loss models of Fishman and Withiam (2011) as the basis for the sacrificial steel thickness of HBSNs. Their work focused on MSE walls, where fill aggressiveness can be controlled by acceptance criteria; the model rests on extensive studies of corrosion rates of uncoated mild steel wire or strips buried in different soils in MSE reinforced zones, was intended to include passive reinforcement embedded in the ground (post-tensioned elements were evaluated separately), and reviewed the variability of steel properties and the accuracy of the models, expressed as reduced resistance factors for tension. As in Chapter 7, for plain steel elements X(um) = 80 (um/yr) x tf^0.8 (Eq. 7.1), with X the loss of steel in um and tf the service life in years; the steel loss is taken twice from the bar diameter, dloss = dbar - 2X (Eq. 7.2), with dloss the diameter after sacrificial steel and dbar the nominal diameter. In the absence of product-specific data these give the diameter reduction over the design life, which is used to calculate the steel area for bar design in Chapter 6; the resistance factors for steel in tension of Chapters 5 and 6 are used for the tendon tensile resistance.
key_points: Fishman and Withiam (2011) metal loss model used for want of soil nail specific studies
Model from uncoated mild steel buried in MSE reinforced zones, where fill aggressiveness is controlled
Eq. 7.1 X(um) = 80 (um/yr) x tf^0.8; Eq. 7.2 dloss = dbar - 2X
Reduced area used in Chapter 6 bar design with the Chapter 5 and 6 tension resistance factors
subsections.applicability: Sacrificial steel allowance for hollow bar soil nails.

subsections.title: Design Steps for Corrosion Protection of HBSNs
subsections.summary: HBSN corrosion design steps: select a trial size; classify the soil with Table 7.2 (HBSNs not recommended in aggressive soil); in non-aggressive soil use Class C (sacrificial steel): nominal diameter, design life (typically 50 to 75 years), sacrificial steel by Eq. 7-1, reduced diameter and area used as At in Eq. 6-5; apply the tension resistance factor to the nominal resistance; compare with the software's tensile forces and repeat as needed.
subsections.body: 10.4.3 Design Steps for Corrosion Protection of HBSNs (p. 269). The selection of corrosion protection for HBSNs uses these steps: (1) select an HBSN trial size; (2) use Table 7.2 to classify the soil as non-aggressive or aggressive, from corrosion testing as described in Chapters 4 and 7; if aggressive, the use of HBSNs is not recommended; (3) if non-aggressive, Class C protection (sacrificial steel) may be used; (4) select Class C: a. obtain the nominal tendon diameter; b. select the design life of the wall (typically 50 to 75 years); c. calculate sacrificial steel using Eq. 7-1 (as printed); d. calculate the new diameter with steel loss; e. use it to calculate the tendon area with steel loss; f. use that area as the tendon cross-sectional area At in Eq. 6-5 to calculate the nominal tendon resistance; g. proceed with the design according to Chapter 6; (5) calculate the factored resistance of the trial HBSN by applying the resistance factor to the nominal tensile resistance (Chapters 5 and 6) with the reduced steel area; (6) compare the nominal resistance (as printed) with the tensile forces from computer-based design software (Chapter 6) and repeat as needed.
key_points: Select a trial HBSN size
Classify the soil with Table 7.2; HBSNs not recommended in aggressive soil
Non-aggressive soil: Class C (sacrificial steel), design life typically 50 to 75 years
Reduced area used as At in Eq. 6-5; factored resistance with the Chapter 5 and 6 factors
Compare with the software's tensile forces and iterate

sections.title: Corrosion Protection Monitoring
sections.summary: Owners should consider corrosion monitoring of HBSNs to check long-term performance and remove excess conservatism. Techniques: buried coupons retrieved through the facing (destructive; lockable openings; localized) and remote electrochemical potential and polarization resistance measurements (nondestructive), used on some coupons to calibrate. Elias et al. (2009) recommend 200 ft maximum spacing for MSE walls; soil nail walls need smaller spacing. Read at installation, monthly for 3 months, bi-monthly for 9 months, then annually.
sections.body: 10.5 Corrosion Protection Monitoring (pp. 269-271). Because HBSNs often save significant cost over solid bars, Owners should consider corrosion monitoring to evaluate long-term HBSN performance, support future corrosion protection developments and eliminate excessive conservatism in the manual's formulation. Goals: (i) assess corrosion rates over years to decades; (ii) confirm or rectify design metal loss assumptions; (iii) investigate performance under changing conditions (e.g., migration of corrosive substances); (iv) furnish data on the integrity of permanent steel-reinforced structures. Monitoring can detect undesired performance where service life estimates were too optimistic, or support extending service life, helping asset management (Elias et al. 2009). Monitoring is uncommon on solid bar soil nail projects but more common for MSE walls; Elias et al. (2009) describe MSE wall corrosion monitoring and DOT programs. Techniques: (i) coupons buried behind the wall during construction, whose retrieval is destructive and needs access through the facing (special detailing with lockable openings planned early), limited to the number of coupons and localized; (ii) remote electrochemical methods, potential and polarization resistance (PR) for instantaneous, average in situ corrosion rates, nondestructive and available at any time; remote methods are recommended on at least some retrievable coupons to confirm and calibrate. Coupons should be placed where corrosion is expected to be faster, under 'normal' conditions as a benchmark, and ideally include carbon steel, zinc and galvanized steel. Locations depend on wall length: Elias et al. (2009) recommend 200 ft maximum spacing for MSE walls; soil nail walls in more variable natural soils should have smaller spacing, with more coupons where corrosion potential is higher; test at different depths and distances from the face (a minimum of two each recommended for MSE walls). Monitor at installation, monthly for 3 months, bi-monthly for the next 9 months, then annually, ideally long enough to see slow initial corrosion under coatings, coating depletion and faster long-term corrosion of the base carbon steel. Results will refine HBSN resistance factors and metal loss models.
key_points: Owners should consider corrosion monitoring of HBSN walls to reduce excess conservatism
Buried coupons: destructive retrieval through the facing; plan lockable openings; localized results
Remote potential and polarization resistance: nondestructive; calibrate on some buried coupons
Coupons where corrosion is faster and under normal conditions; carbon steel, zinc, galvanized
Elias et al. (2009): 200 ft maximum spacing for MSE walls; smaller spacing for soil nail walls
At least two depths and two distances from the face (MSE wall recommendation)
Readings at installation, monthly 3 months, bi-monthly 9 months, then annually
